title: The Hunter
text:
Long ago, people told stories about Orion, a strong and skilled hunter.

He walked through forests and over hills, following the tracks animals left behind. He could wait quietly until he found what he was looking for. Each hunt made him more sure of his strength.

Soon, Orion believed he was the greatest hunter of all. He said he could kill any animal on Earth. He thought no creature could stop him.

But his words angered Gaia, the goddess of the Earth. Orion was about to face an animal he had never feared: a scorpion.
marginNotes: Remember these three close stars. You will look for them later.
glaux: Even a great hunter has something left to learn.

title: The Scorpion
text:
Gaia was the goddess of the Earth in Greek myth. In this story, she was angry because Orion said he could kill any animal.

She sent a scorpion to face him.

Orion saw it near his feet. Its tail curved over its back, ready to sting. The hunter trusted his strength, just as he always had.

Then the scorpion stung him, and Orion died. His hunting journeys had come to an end.

His strength could not save him. Yet people would remember the hunter in a surprising place: the night sky.
marginNotes: There are different versions of this myth. Here, a scorpion kills Orion.
glaux: His strength could not protect him from the sting.

title: Among the Stars
text:
In this myth, Zeus, the ruler of the gods, placed the scorpion in the sky.

Artemis, the goddess of the hunt, cared about Orion. She wanted him to be remembered too, and asked Zeus to give him a place among the stars.

So Orion became a hunter in the night sky. The story gave both the hunter and the scorpion a place among the stars.

Look at the picture. His arm is raised, and a belt crosses his waist. People imagined this shape when they looked at the stars.

They did not see a real person in the sky. They joined bright points into a picture, then gave that picture a story.
marginNotes: The hunter is a drawing. The chart shows where the stars appear from Earth.
glaux: The story gives us a picture. Now let us find its stars.

title: Look Up
text:
Now look at the star chart. A star chart is a map of the sky.

Near the middle, three bright stars sit close together, almost in a straight line. They form the belt in the picture of Orion.

From the belt, look up towards his shoulders. The reddish star at one shoulder is called Betelgeuse.

The hunter is part of the myth. The stars are real, faraway suns. The lines help us see a shape; they are not real lines in space.

Start with those three belt stars. You now know a simple way to recognise Orion.
glaux: Find the belt first. Then look for the shoulders.

title: A family on the road
text:
Long ago, storytellers told of seven sisters who travelled with their mother, Pleione. Their father was Atlas, a powerful figure from Greek myth.

One day, Pleione and her daughters were passing through Boeotia, a region of Greece. Imagine a road winding between hills, with the family walking together.

Their journey was about to change. A hunter named Orion was near.

title: Orion approaches
text:
Orion was a hunter, known in Greek stories for his great strength. In this telling, he became a threat to Pleione and her family.

He tried to grab Pleione. She did not want him near her. She escaped, and he followed.

What had begun as a journey through the countryside had become an escape. Pleione and her daughters needed to get away.

title: Keeping together
text:
Pleione fled, with Orion following. In this retelling, we picture her daughters staying close as the family escaped.

Imagine them moving through the hills as daylight faded. One sister might watch the path ahead while another looked behind.

The road in our picture is imagined. What the old account tells us is simpler: Pleione escaped, and Orion could not find her.

title: Seven passing years
text:
Orion did not give up his search. The old account says he looked for Pleione for seven years, without finding her.

Imagine the seasons returning: new leaves, warm days, falling leaves, bare branches. The family had escaped his reach, but the long search continued.

Then the story turns away from Orion and towards the sisters.
glaux: Even an old story can leave some paths unmarked.

title: Zeus takes notice
text:
Zeus, king of the gods, saw the daughters and felt pity for them. He decided to give them a place among the stars.

This is where the tale leaves the roads and hills behind. A god could lift the sisters into the night sky, beyond the world where their journey began.

The next time people looked up, they could imagine the sisters there together.

title: A place among the stars
text:
Zeus placed the seven sisters among the stars. The story gave them a new place in the night: a small gathering of lights.

Imagine looking up after following their journey. The sisters are no longer figures on a distant road. They are the little group shining overhead.

People remembered them as the Pleiades, the Seven Sisters. But the telling has one final turn.

title: The sky remembers
text:
In this version, Orion still seems to follow the sisters across the sky. The hunter and the little group of lights remain part of the same imagined chase.

That chase belongs to the story. The real stars are not hunting or running from one another.

The sisters stay together in the telling. Now we can leave the myth and meet the real lights that inspired it.
glaux: Let the tale rest. Now meet the lights themselves.
